text: An alloy's nominal composition specifies which elements are present and their relative amounts under a stated composition convention. It does not uniquely specify grain size, phase fractions, texture, defects, or processing history. Two samples with the same nominal composition may therefore show different mechanical behavior. Composition and material state should be recorded separately when comparing experiments.

High-entropy alloys are often discussed in terms of configurational entropy, but entropy alone does not guarantee a single stable solid solution. Mixing enthalpy, temperature, ordering, competing phases and kinetic constraints can also influence the observed microstructure. A claim about phase stability should identify the conditions and evidence rather than rely only on the number of alloying elements.

The equiatomic Cantor alloy contains cobalt, chromium, iron, manganese and nickel. Its composition may be written with the element symbols in a different order without changing the atomic fractions. This convention should not be confused with a statement about identical heat treatment or mechanical properties. A formula describes composition, while experimental history describes how a particular specimen was produced.

In a tensile test, a specimen is pulled while force and deformation are measured. Stress is related to applied force and cross-sectional area, and strain characterizes relative deformation. Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation describe different aspects of the response. Values should be reported together with test temperature, strain rate, specimen geometry and the definition of the measured quantity.

X-ray diffraction can help identify crystalline phases, while electron microscopy can reveal features of the microstructure at selected length scales. Neither method should be treated as a substitute for every other characterization technique. Interpretation depends on resolution, sampling, signal quality and the assumptions of the analysis. Complementary measurements can provide a more complete description of a material.

Atomic percent and weight percent use different composition bases. Conversion between them requires the atomic masses of the constituent elements. A formula written as relative atomic coefficients can be normalized by dividing each coefficient by their sum. Multiplying all coefficients by the same positive factor leaves the normalized atomic fractions unchanged, but changing just one coefficient usually changes the composition.
